title: Block close: the house of prayer
hookLine: rites and rooms, bells and bread: faith lives in places and bodies

cards: Lay out what this stretch of days has put in your hands. Water poured at a font. Oil on a forehead.
Bread broken and a cup passed. A bell in a tower. Incense rising.
A candle left burning. A hymnal with a cracked spine. Chalk above a door.
A shelf in the corner of a room. A boot on a road in Spain. Every one is something you can touch, smell, hear or walk.

teach.h: RITES: SOMETHING DONE WITH A BODY.
teach.b: First, the rites. Baptism. Chrismation and confirmation.

First communion. The Divine Liturgy and the Mass, a Protestant service, a Quaker meeting held in silence, a Pentecostal service full of sound. The sermon, the creed said together, the peace, the offering, the blessing.
Weddings, ordination, anointing the sick, confession, vows. Churches disagree about how many sacraments there are and what happens in them.
But each rite does something with a body: water, oil, hands, a bowed head, a handshake of peace. Second, the rooms. The basilica's long hall.
The iconostasis, a wall of faces. The gothic cathedral pulling light upward. The plain meeting house with nothing on the walls.
Domes like a sky. The table, the pulpit and the font, each set where it is for a reason.

teach.h: ROOMS: A SENTENCE IN STONE AND WOOD.
teach.b: A room is a sentence about God, in stone and wood.

teach.h: ARTS AND THINGS, CHURCH AND HOME.
teach.b: Third, the arts and the things: bells and the colors of the year, incense and candles, the cross and the crucifix, icons, hymnals, organs, guitars and drums, choirs, churches and crosses from around the world.
Then the home: name days, grace at meals, bedtime prayers, the icon corner, the blessing on the door. Then the road: the Camino and the retreat. Last, the title.

teach.h: A HOUSE OF PRAYER FOR ALL PEOPLE.
teach.b: Isaiah: "for mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people." Jesus quotes it in the temple, in Mark.

And Paul carries the idea into the body: "What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you?" A building can be a house of prayer; so can a kitchen; and Paul calls the body a temple.

how: Christians pray in churches, chapels and meeting houses shaped by their traditions, and at home in prayer corners, at tables and at bedsides; the rites of each church use water, bread, oil, hands, music and silence.

games.q: you're Jesus, walking into the temple court. it's crowded with money changers and people selling doves. what do you do?
o: walk past them and pray quietly in a corner.
overturn the tables, and quote Isaiah: a house of prayer.
raise it with the priests some other day.
games.why: in Mark, he overturns the tables and says it is written: my house shall be called of all nations the house of prayer.

practice: Bring to mind one place where prayer, or quiet, or love has been real for you, a church, a grandmother's kitchen, a hospital chapel, a bench by the water, and see the light, the sounds, who was there, and what your body did: kneel, sit, sing, cry, stand still.
If you pray, you can thank God for that place; if you don't, let yourself be glad it exists.
